answer.rationale: Finance mandates an 18% cost cut. The incumbent contract expires in 14 days and does not auto-renew, so an immediate decision is forced. The assembly line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, so any move that risks delivery disruption is unacceptable. Memory c4 directly evidences that renegotiating at renewal recovered real margin by benchmarking market rates and shifting both price and payment terms. Memory c1 shows renewing with the incumbent preserves integration stability across cycles with no migration work and no interruption to scheduled deliveries. Since we have capacity for exactly one action this cycle, I will not consume the verification budget; instead I will negotiate terms with the incumbent, using c4 as the playbook (benchmark and push on price + payment terms) and c1 as the safety argument (incumbent renewal protects delivery). This minimizes TCO without increasing delivery risk because the supply continuity is preserved while targeting the mandated 18% reduction. A full vendor switch or onboarding a second source would be higher-risk and slower, which the 94% no-buffer throughput cannot absorb. The non-critical deferral pattern from memory c5 is not applicable here because the contract does not auto-renew; inaction means losing the relationship and inviting disruption. I am not pulling any archive verification this cycle because both supporting memories are recent (days 21 and 29) and internally consistent with the situation; saving the budget for the next review where it may matter more.
